after.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =5x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡10x={cos}^{2}⁡5x-{sin}^{2}⁡5x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{x}^{2}+10{sin}^{2}⁡5x-10{cos}^{2}⁡5x)\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-10({cos}^{2}⁡5x-{sin}^{2}⁡5x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}-10\operatorname{cos}⁡10x)\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}-10(\frac{1}{10}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡10x)+C \\  & ={x}^{3}-\operatorname{sin}⁡10x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)={sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({sin}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$
